title: Iron-based superconductor wire fabrication
bottleneck: Iron pnictides and chalcogenides offer high upper critical fields and lower anisotropy than cuprates, yet no one has produced long-length iron-based wire with competitive current density. The materials are brittle, sensitive to stoichiometry, and their grain boundaries suppress supercurrent even more sharply than in cuprates. Powder-in-tube routes that worked for other superconductors have yielded only modest results.
why_it_blocks: Iron-based conductors could undercut REBCO on cost for high-field magnets while operating at more forgiving temperatures than low-Tc niobium alloys. Without a viable wire process, this entire material family stays in the lab while magnet builders pay premium prices for alternatives.
current_state: Research continues on 122-type and 11-type compounds with improved grain-boundary engineering, but commercial wire remains absent. The field's attention has largely shifted to REBCO and hydrides, leaving iron-based conductor development underfunded relative to its potential.
